title: Russia to Take 70,000 Indian Skilled Workers This Year, Jaishankar Tells Parliament Panel
excerpt: The external affairs minister's briefing covered trade, energy and Ukraine diplomacy — plus India's push to bring home citizens recruited into Russia's military.
body:
• External affairs minister S. Jaishankar told a parliamentary consultative committee on Saturday that Russia has agreed to take around 70,000 Indian skilled workers this year, mainly in construction and logistics, according to PTI.
  • The minister said India and Russia aim to expand trade in a more balanced manner, targeting Indian exports across seven sectors — automobiles, pharmaceuticals, food, marine products, engineering goods, chemicals and textiles.
  • Indians considering work in Russia should use registered recruitment channels and verify job offers: the government says about 140 Indians have been discharged from the Russian military and it is tracing 55 more, with action being taken against fraudulent recruiters.
  • On energy, Jaishankar said India's priority is protecting domestic consumers by maintaining multiple sources of supply.

External affairs minister S. Jaishankar briefed a parliamentary consultative committee on Saturday on India's "multifaceted" engagement with Russia, covering bilateral trade, investment and energy cooperation — and informing members that Russia has agreed to take around 70,000 Indian skilled workers this year, particularly in construction and logistics.

Chairing the meeting on India-Russia relations, Jaishankar said India and Russia share an ambition to expand bilateral trade in a more balanced manner, including by increasing Indian exports to Russia across seven sectors — automobiles, pharmaceuticals, food, marine products, engineering goods, chemicals and textiles, people familiar with the discussions told PTI.

Trade, connectivity and energy cooperation

The minister highlighted various areas of bilateral engagement, including trade, investments, energy, connectivity, culture and people-to-people ties, according to a social media post by Jaishankar. The discussions also covered an India-Eurasian Economic Union Free Trade Agreement, the Chennai-Vladivostok corridor, the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) and the Northern Sea Route.

On energy cooperation, Jaishankar said India's priority was to safeguard the interests of Indian consumers. "Our approach is to maintain multiple sources of supply," he said, according to people familiar with the meeting. The government has also been seeking to expand opportunities for Indian workers in Russia.

Ukraine conflict and India's diplomacy

The Ukraine conflict featured prominently in the discussions, with Jaishankar apprising the panel of India's position and recent diplomatic efforts to support dialogue and diplomacy. In his social media post, Jaishankar said he highlighted India's "active support to dialogue and diplomacy to end the Ukraine conflict."

The minister referred to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's August 31 meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Bishkek, where the prime minister said that "endless war must now give way to end of war." Jaishankar travelled to Ukraine last month and subsequently met the foreign ministers of Ukraine and Russia in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, conveying India's readiness to assist efforts to bring the conflict to an end.

"If India can be of any help in any manner to bring the war to an end, it is ready to do so."

— S. Jaishankar, in conversations with Ukrainian and Russian foreign ministers

Putin's recent remarks at the Valdai Club in Moscow were also discussed. He had said Prime Minister Modi "has very good ideas for finding mutually acceptable solutions" to bring peace. Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha's remarks appreciating India's efforts were also noted during the meeting.

Efforts to bring Indians home from Russia's military

Jaishankar also briefed the committee on the government's efforts to secure the release of Indian nationals serving in the Russian military. The government has engaged with Russian authorities, including at the highest levels, for the early discharge of such individuals. So far, around 140 Indian nationals have been discharged, while India is in touch with Russian authorities regarding the whereabouts of 55 Indian nationals who are reportedly working for the Russian army.

The government has also been taking action against agents who recruit Indians for such roles, with committee members being briefed about the risks faced by Indian citizens joining the Russian army.

What this means for Indian workers

The 70,000-worker figure is significant: Russia's economy faces acute labour shortages in construction and logistics as the Ukraine war drags on, and Moscow has increasingly looked to India to fill the gap. For prospective Indian migrants, the opportunity comes with a clear caution from New Delhi — verify every offer, use only government-registered recruitment channels, and understand the distinction between civilian contract work and military enlistment schemes pushed by unscrupulous agents.

What's next

The India-EAEU free trade agreement talks, the freight corridors and the worker pipeline will be the metrics to watch in the coming months. For India, the balancing act remains the same: deepening the Russia relationship on trade and labour mobility while preserving diplomatic space on Ukraine and protecting its own citizens caught in the war's orbit.
